opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the distinction is a lot blurrier than people expect, and on our team we've deliberately tried not to make too much of it.

The rough historical picture is that research scientists come up with ideas, design experiments, and figure out what to try next, while research engineers build the infrastructure, write the training code, and make things run at scale. That was probably a more meaningful split in earlier eras of machine learning, when a lot of progress came from clever new algorithms you could test on a single GPU.

But the way ML research works now, especially with large language models, an enormous share of the actual work is engineering. You're dealing with huge codebases, distributed training, getting runs to be stable, debugging why some loss curve looks weird, building evaluation pipelines. And often the bottleneck on whether an idea works isn't the idea itself. It's whether someone can implement it carefully, run the experiment cleanly, and interpret the results correctly. A lot of the most impactful people I've worked with are, by background, engineers. They have very good research taste because they've spent so much time close to the actual systems.

So in practice, on the alignment team, research engineers and research scientists do pretty similar things day to day. Everyone writes code, everyone runs experiments, everyone is expected to think about what the results mean and what we should do next. The difference is more about emphasis and the path people took to get here. Someone with a PhD and a publication record might come in with the "scientist" title. Someone who's been a strong software engineer and picked up ML might come in as a "research engineer." But once they're on the team, the boundary dissolves quickly.

The practical upshot for people listening: if you're a strong engineer who cares about alignment, don't think you need a PhD before you can contribute to research. There's a huge amount of really important work that's mostly a matter of good engineering plus good judgment. And if you're more on the science side, getting your hands dirty with engineering will make you a much better researcher, because you'll develop intuitions for what's actually feasible and what the systems are really doing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the distinction is a lot blurrier than people outside tend to assume. When I first got into the field, I kind of pictured it as: the research scientists come up with the ideas and the research engineers implement them. And that's really not how it works, at least not on the teams I've been on.

In practice, almost everyone on the alignment team does some mix of both. If you're a research scientist, you're still writing a lot of code — you're building experiments, you're debugging training runs, you're looking at data. And if you're a research engineer, you're not just taking a spec and executing on it; you're making tons of judgment calls about what to try, what to measure, why something isn't working, and those are fundamentally research decisions.

So the way I'd put it is that it's more of a difference in center of gravity than a hard line. A research scientist is maybe more likely to be the person asking "what question should we be asking here, and what experiment would actually answer it?" And a research engineer is maybe more likely to be the person who makes the thing actually work at scale, who thinks about the infrastructure and the systems and how to get something that runs on one GPU to run across a whole cluster without falling over. And at a place like OpenAI, where so much of the progress depends on being able to run things at scale, that second skill set is enormously valuable — I'd honestly say it's often the bottleneck.

The other thing I'd say is that the job titles are partly historical. They came from a world where the PhD was the credential you needed to be called a scientist. But some of the best researchers I've worked with don't have PhDs and came in through the engineering track, and they're generating research ideas and running the experiments and writing the papers just like anyone else. So I'd encourage people not to get too hung up on which title they're going for. The more important question is: can you take a vague, fuzzy problem, turn it into something concrete you can actually test, and then build the thing and find out? If you can do that, you'll be useful regardless of what it says on your badge.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as more of a spectrum than a sharp distinction. On the research engineering side, the emphasis is on making experiments work: implementing ideas, getting the infrastructure right, and making sure you can run things reliably and understand the results. On the research science side, there’s more emphasis on deciding which questions to ask, developing hypotheses, and figuring out what experiments would distinguish between them.

But in practice, those are very intertwined. When you implement something, you often discover that your original idea wasn’t quite right, or you notice something that suggests a new research direction. And to choose good experiments, you need to understand what’s actually feasible to build. So I wouldn’t draw the distinction as one person having the ideas and another person writing the code. Both contribute to the research; they just tend to have different strengths.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a spectrum rather than a sharp distinction. Research engineers tend to focus more on making experiments work: implementing ideas, building the infrastructure, and getting things to run efficiently and reliably. Research scientists tend to focus more on deciding which questions to investigate, forming hypotheses, and designing experiments to test them.

But there’s a lot of overlap. You might start implementing an idea and realise that the experiment needs to be designed differently, or discover something that suggests a new research direction. And as a research scientist, you still need to understand the implementation well enough to know what your results actually mean. So in practice, people often do some of both, with different strengths and different emphases.
